groups.title: Styling Approaches
groups.question: Your app's CSS has grown into thousands of lines with unused rules and class names that clash between components. Explain how Tailwind or CSS Modules would solve this.

followUps.Utility-first with Tailwind: With Tailwind, what do you do when the same set of classes repeats in many places?
followUps.CSS Modules: How do CSS Modules stop two components' .title classes from clashing?

evidence.text: Tailwind styles elements with small single-purpose classes written in the markup.
This avoids naming classes and leaves no unused CSS behind, since only used classes are generated.
Repeated patterns are extracted into a reusable component, not into new CSS classes.

notEnough: Only saying Tailwind is faster to write.

evidence.text: CSS Modules rename class names at build time so they are unique to their file.
Styles in one component cannot accidentally affect another.
You still write normal CSS, just without global collisions.

notEnough: Only saying CSS Modules are local styles.

groups.title: Design Tokens
groups.question: Marketing wants a new brand color and a dark mode, and today the old color is hard-coded in 200 places. Explain how design tokens and theming would make this a one-line change.

followUps.Tokens as CSS variables: What is a design token, and why define tokens as CSS variables?
followUps.Theming and dark mode: How would you switch to dark mode and respect the user's system setting?

evidence.text: Design tokens are named values for colors, spacing and type sizes.
Defining them once as CSS variables means changing a token updates every use.
Tokens give designers and developers a shared vocabulary.
Changing the token variables on the root element switches the whole theme.
prefers-color-scheme lets you follow the user's system setting by default.
Users should still be able to choose a theme that overrides the default.

notEnough: Only saying you would add a dark class.

groups.title: Components
groups.question: You are building a shared Button and a Dialog for your team's component library. Explain how you would design their options and make sure they are accessible.

followUps.Variants and composition: Why give a Button a few variants like size and intent instead of accepting any style?
followUps.Headless, accessible primitives: Why use a headless library like Radix for a dialog instead of building it from scratch?

evidence.text: A small set of named variants keeps the UI consistent.
Accepting arbitrary styles lets every screen drift from the design.
A helper like class-variance-authority maps each variant to its classes in one place.

notEnough: Only listing variants without explaining why they are limited.

evidence.text: Headless libraries provide the behavior and accessibility of dialogs, menus and tabs.
That includes focus handling, keyboard support and screen reader attributes that are easy to get wrong.
They do not impose a look, so you style them with your own design.

groups.title: Documentation
groups.question: Designers keep finding small spacing and color differences between screens, and a refactor once changed button styles across the app without anyone noticing. Explain how you would document components and keep the UI consistent.

followUps.Storybook: What does Storybook give a team that a running app does not?
followUps.Visual consistency checks: How would you catch an accidental style change before it reaches users?

evidence.text: Storybook shows each component on its own, outside the app.
It shows every variant and state, including rare ones like errors.
That makes components easy to review, test and hand off to designers.
Shared spacing and type scales keep screens consistent.
Using shared components instead of one-off styles prevents drift.
Visual regression tests compare screenshots and flag unexpected changes.

notEnough: Only saying you would review it manually.
